title: Montaigne travels
hook: Montaigne loved travel for the new and the different (Essays 3.9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends, women, books, and your line was three companies. Did you give a little time to each one? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

A traveler stands at a fork in the road. On the right, the way looks ugly. So he takes the left. That's the whole plan. No map marked in red, no list of sights, no deadline. If he gets somewhere he doesn't like, he leaves; if he forgets to see something, he goes back. This is Montaigne on the road, in a long, wandering essay of book three called Of vanity. The same man who retreated to a tower full of books also loved to leave it. Today, why.
screen: `UGLY ON THE RIGHT? GO LEFT.` → `NO PLAN, NO DEADLINE.` → `THE TOWER MAN LEAVES HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the plan that isn't one. Montaigne describes travel without a fixed route. He isn't chasing a destination, so he can't be late for it. The road itself is the point. Second, the new and the different. He says travel is good exercise for the mind, which is kept busy noticing things it hasn't seen before. Other people's ways of eating, dressing and greeting: all of it shows him the wide variety of human lives, and loosens the grip of his own habits. Third, the travelers he laughs at. He pokes fun at people who go abroad only to find their own countrymen, eat their own food, and complain about everything foreign. To him that misses the point of going. He would rather sit at a stranger's table and eat what they eat. Fourth, the honest answer. People ask him what he is looking for on these trips. He answers, more or less, that he knows well what he's fleeing, but not what he's seeking. It's a strangely freeing confession. Not every journey needs a goal written down before it begins. Sometimes it's enough to know you need a change of air and to trust the road to show you something. None of this needs a plane. A different street to the store, a different bench at lunch, a neighborhood you always drive past. The mind wakes up a little when it meets something it didn't expect.
screen: `NO FIXED ROUTE.` · `EXERCISE FOR THE MIND.` · `DON'T GO ABROAD TO FIND HOME.` · `I KNOW WHAT I FLEE, NOT WHAT I SEEK.` · then, large: `A NEW ROUTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a new route, and then let go of the plan. Sit, and breathe. Picture a trip you make most days: to work, to the store, to the mailbox. Now picture one small change: a different turn, a different street, a different door. Don't pick a destination; just pick the turn. Then let your mind wander down that unfamiliar street for a while, curious, the way Montaigne's did. If it drifts back to the usual road, take the left again. The bell holds the time.
Montaigne travels. No fixed route, a stranger's table, and a mind kept awake by the new. Today's word.
Your line: a new route. Today, take one different turn on a trip you always make, and notice one thing you've never seen there. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of vanity often take from it his love of unplanned travel, his curiosity about other people's customs, and his line about knowing what he flees but not what he seeks.

fork.setup: you're on the road with Montaigne and the way ahead looks ugly. what does he do?
options: push on; the plan is the plan.
fork.reveal: if it looks bad on the right, he goes left. there's no fixed route to be late for.

trapdoor: what you thought: an essay called Of vanity would be about pride.
what it means: it wanders through travel, change and restlessness, and why Montaigne loves the road.
what a scholar hears: the essay itself rambles on purpose, its form matching his unplanned journeys.

notes: Essays 3.9 is paraphrased throughout; no English translation was quoted.
